facts.statement: The origin of the holotype specimen CM 2815 is uncertain, with conflicting reports placing it in either the Belle Fourche Shale or the Hailey Shales Formation.
facts.quote: The holotype, CM 2815, origin is uncertain, the original paper says it is from Belle Fourche Shale in the Rattlesnake Hills of Wyoming (lower Cenomanian), but the Carnegie Museum collections data says its from the Hailey Shales Formation.

facts.statement: The holotype appears to be the only known fossil of the genus Plesiopleurodon.
facts.quote: Regardless of its origin, it seems to be the only known fossil of Plesiopleurodon.

facts.statement: The skull of Plesiopleurodon measures 71.2 cm in length.
The eight caniniform teeth in Plesiopleurodon tilt forward and are smooth except for striations near their attachment to the jaw.
facts.quote: The eight caniniform teeth are procumbent, or tilt forward, and smooth but are striated near where they attach to the jaw.

facts.statement: The cervical ribs of Plesiopleurodon have a single head, a trait shared with other Cretaceous pliosaurs.
facts.quote: Like other Cretaceous pliosaurs, the cervical ribs have one head.

facts.statement: The species is characterized by a moderately long symphysis bearing 8 pairs of nearly circular, smooth teeth, single-headed cervical ribs, and a long, thin interpectoral bar on the coracoids.
facts.quote: La especie es caracterizada por una sínfisis moderadamente larga que lleva 8 pares de dientes, los dientes que son casi circulares en sección transversal y lisos en la superficie externa (excepto cerca de la base), las costillas de las vértebras cervicales poseen una única cabeza (son de doble cabeza en los pliosaurios jurásicos) y por una barra interpectoral larga y delgada en los coracoides.

facts.statement: Carpenter noted that Plesiopleurodon wellesi most closely resembles the European Oxfordian species Liopleurodon ferox.
facts.quote: It was named by Kenneth Carpenter based on a complete skull with a mandible, cervical vertebra, and a coracoid. In naming the specimen, Carpenter noted "Of all known pliosauroids, Plesiopleurodon wellesi most closely resembles Liopleurodon ferox from the Oxfordian of Europe, hence the generic reference."

facts.statement: The animal was initially described as a pliosauroid because of its short neck, although it belongs to the order Plesiosauria.
facts.quote: It was initially described as a pliosauroid due to it short neck, a common trait of the superfamily (although it is in the order Plesiosauria).

facts.statement: Later research classifies Plesiopleurodon as a member of the family Polycotylidae within the clade Occultonectia.
facts.quote: Later research indicates it is a member of the Polycotylidae, within the clade Occultonectia.

facts.statement: In 2018, Fischer and colleagues named the clade Occultonectia to include Plesiopleurodon, the Richmond pliosaur, and Sulcusuchus erraini.
facts.quote: Fischer and colleagues, in 2018, named a new clade, Occultonectia, to include Plesiopleurodon, the 'Richmond pliosaur' (museum number QM F18041), and Sulcusuchus erraini.

facts.statement: Plesiopleurodon lived during the Cenomanian stage, approximately 100.5 to 93.9 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Cenomanian to Cenomanian (100.5 to 93.9 million years ago)

facts.statement: Only one fossil occurrence of Plesiopleurodon has been recorded.
Plesiopleurodon was an obligatory aquatic animal that swam using paraxial propulsion from paddle-like flippers, similar to sea turtles.
facts.quote: Plesiopleurodon, like all plesiosaurs, are obligatory aquatic animals that rely on paraxial propulsion to swim. This means locomotion depends on the propulsion from paddle-like flippers, much like how sea turtles move.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the short neck of Plesiopleurodon definitively places it in the pliosauroid group, as later research shows neck length varies within both plesiosauroids and pliosauroids.
facts.quote: However, later exploration into the relationships of both groups indicate that not all pliosauroids have short necks and not all plesiosauroids have long necks.

rejected.statement: The genus was named by Kenneth Carpenter in 1996 based on a single specimen containing a complete skull, mandible, cervical vertebra, and coracoid.
rejected.quote: It was named by Kenneth Carpenter based on a complete skull with a mandible, cervical vertebra, and a coracoid.
